extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors of plane and spherical trigonometry; advanced geometry readers
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, lemmas, propositions, and solution-cases for plane and spherical trigonometry: includes measures of angles, sine/tangent/secant definitions, key trig propositions for plane triangles, solution procedures for right and oblique triangles, and initial spherical-trigonometry definitions and propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem I (Euclid's Data)
rubrics_metrics.description: To find three straight lines such, that the ratio of the first to the second is given; and if a given straight line be taken from the second, the ratio of the remainder to the third is given; also the rectangle contained by the first and third is given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: label AB first, CD second, EF third. Use given ratios and a given segment BH to reduce to known proportions; form a rectangle BA·AH equal to given rectangle AB·EF and apply proportional constructions (references to props. 24, 29, etc.). The composition shows making KL:KM correspond to AB:CD etc., and demonstrates equality of rectangles and given ratios to deduce AB, CD, EF.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem II (Euclid's Data)
rubrics_metrics.description: To find three straight lines such, that the ratio of the first to the second is given; and if a given straight line be taken from the second, the ratio of the remainder to the third is given; also the sum of the squares of the first and third is given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: let AB first, BC second, BD third. Use given ratios and a given AE to relate EB to BD, place BD at right angles to EB and join DE to get triangle EBD given in species so angle is given. Use given sum of squares to fix AD (square of AD is given), locate point D as intersection of given AD and ED in position; then DB perpendicular to AB gives B. Composition: choose segments FG:GB to match AB:BC, place GL at right angles and construct circle with centre A radius AN equal to required square; intersections yield D and consequently AB, BC, BD (references to figures and earlier props).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma I (Measure relation angle/arc)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ABC be a rectilineal angle; if about point B as centre and with any distance BA a circle be described meeting BA, BC in A, C, the angle ABC will be to four right angles as the arch AC to the whole circumference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: extend AB to meet circle again in F; draw DE perpendicular to AB meeting circle; use previous results (33.6 Elem.) and quadrupling to equate ratios of angle to four right angles with arc AC to full circumference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma II (Arc equivalence across circles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two circles described about the same centre with distances BD, BA meeting BA, BC in D,E and A,C respectively, the arch AC is to the whole circumference of which it is an arch as the arch DE is to the whole circumference of which it is an arch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Lemma I twice: both arches relate to the same angle ABC and hence are proportional to their circumferences in the same ratio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition I (Measure of an angle)
rubrics_metrics.description: If about B as centre with BA any distance a circle ACF be described meeting BA, BC in A, C, the arch AC is called the measure of the angle ABC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines angle measure by arc on any circle centered at the angle vertex; corollary: choice of radius does not change the number of degrees of the arc (Lemma 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition II (Degrees/minutes/seconds)
rubrics_metrics.description: The circumference of a circle is supposed to be divided into 360 equal parts called degrees, each degree into 60 minutes, each minute into 60 seconds, &c.; as many degrees, minutes, seconds, etc. as are contained in an arch, so many are contained in the angle of which that arch is the measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary: regardless of radius, the arc corresponding to a given angle contains the same number of degrees/minutes/seconds (follows from Lemma II).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition III (Supplement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If AB be produced to meet the circle again in E, the angle CBF, which together with ABC is equal to two right angles, is called the Supplement of angle ABC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplement relates to arc and circle construction; used to define co-functions in later corollaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition IV (Sine of an angle)
rubrics_metrics.description: A straight line CD drawn through C, one extremity of the arch AC perpendicular upon the diameter passing through the other extremity A, is called the Sine of the arch AC, or of the angle ABC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary: sine of a quadrant (a right angle) equals the radius. This geometric definition sets up sine as a chord/segment length relative to radius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition V (Versed sine)
rubrics_metrics.description: The segment DA of the diameter passing through A, one extremity of the arch AC between the sine CD and that extremity, is called the Versed Sine of the arch AC, or angle ABC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Versed sine is the complementary segment of the diameter associated to sine; used in later formulae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition VI (Tangent)
rubrics_metrics.description: A straight line AE touching the circle at A and meeting the diameter BC (through the other extremity C) in E is called the Tangent of the arch AC or of the angle ABC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric tangent defined via tangent line at point A intersecting diameter through opposite extremity; will be used to relate sides and tangents in right/plane triangles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition VII (Secant)
rubrics_metrics.description: The straight line BE between the centre and the extremity of the tangent AE is called the Secant of the arch AC or angle ABC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secant is the line from centre to tangent intersection; corollary notes sine/tangent/secant of an angle and its supplement relate in simple ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary (radius scaling of trig functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sine, versed sine, tangent, and secant of any arch which is the measure of an angle are to the corresponding functions of any other arch measuring the same angle as the radii of the respective circles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows trig functions scale linearly with the chosen circle radius; justifies using tables that assume a fixed radius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition VIII (Complement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference of an angle from a right angle is called the complement of that angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to co-functions: sine/co-sine, tangent/co-tangent, secant/co-secant relative definitions; provides geometric construction (perpendicular) to define complement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition IX (Co-functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: For complement CBH of ABC, the tangent HK (or equal DB) is called the co-tangent, BD the co-sine, and BK the co-secant of the angle ABC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollaries: radius is mean proportional between tangent and co-tangent, and between co-sine and secant; these geometric mean relations are proven via similar triangles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition I (Right-triangle radius relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a right-angled plane triangle, if the hypotenuse be made radius, the sides become the sines of the angles opposite to them; if either side be made radius, the remaining side is the tangent of the angle opposite to it and the hypotenuse the secant of the same angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: draw circles with radii equal to hypotenuse or side; use definitions to identify corresponding sine/tangent/secant relations. Corollaries: given hypotenuse and one acute angle, other parts are determined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition II (Sides proportional to sines)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sides of a plane triangle are to one another as the sines of the angles opposite to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by dropping perpendiculars and using similarity of right triangles; corollary: given two sides and two opposite angles, other elements can be deduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition III (Sum/difference relation via tangents)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a plane triangle, the sum of any two sides is to their difference as the tangent of half the sum of the base angles is to the tangent of half their difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction uses a circle about one vertex and inscribed angles; identifies tangents to half-sum and half-difference of base angles, and relates EC (sum of sides) to CF (difference of sides) via EB/BG tangents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition IV (Side ratios and tangents of excess)
rubrics_metrics.description: In any plane triangle with sides BA (less) and AC (greater), BA:AC is as the radius to the tangent of an angle; and radius to tangent of the excess of that angle above half a right angle is as the tangent of half the sum of base angles to tangent of half their difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction duplicates sides and uses right-angle and similar triangles arguments; shows relations of side ratios to tangents of certain constructed angles (excess over half-right-angle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition V (Rectangle and cosine relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: In any plane triangle, twice the rectangle contained by any two sides is to the difference of the sum of the squares of those two sides and the square of the base as the radius is to the co-sine of the included angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses altitude AD and identities (Props 12,13 of Elem); relates 2·(BA·BC) to (AB^2 + BC^2 - AC^2) and then to radius:cosine via right-triangle sine complement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition VI (Half-perimeter rectangle and tangent relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: In any plane triangle, the rectangle contained by half the perimeter and the excess of it above the base is to the rectangle contained by the straight lines by which the half perimeter exceeds the other two sides as the square of the radius is to the square of the tangent of half the opposite angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses incenter G, equal perpendiculars from incenter, relations among segments AH, AL equal to half-perimeter, and equal rectangles via similar triangles; concludes HAD (half-perimeter × excess over base) relates to square(radius)/square(tan(½ angle)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition VII (Base vs sides via base segments)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a plane triangle, the base is to the sum of the sides as the difference of the sides is to the sum or difference of the segments of the base made by the perpendicular from the vertex, according as the square of the greater side is greater or less than the sum of the squares of the lesser side and the base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct circle about greater side and consider points where altitude meets base or its extension; use rectangle equalities to obtain proportional relation BC:(BA+AC) :: (BA−AC):(BD±DC), depending on which square inequality holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition VIII / Problem (sum and difference given)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the sum and difference of two magnitudes, to find them: half the given sum plus half the given difference is the greater; half the sum minus half the difference is the less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple arithmetic construction: let AB be given sum, constructs AD half sum and add/subtract half difference to get greater and lesser magnitudes; immediate corollary to algebraic decomposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium (Solving triangles — general frame)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the six parts of a plane triangle (three sides and three angles) any three being given, to find the other three is the business of plane trigonometry; special cases may be resolved by preceding propositions and trigonometrical tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides overview and reduction to fourth proportionals or arithmetic via trig tables; introduces table abbreviations: U for Radius, T for Tangent, S for Sine, and notation for degrees/minutes/seconds.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Proposition (right-angled triangle cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a right-angled triangle, of the three sides and three angles, any two being given besides the right angle, the other three may be found, except when the two acute angles are given (only ratios of sides are then given).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References Prop I and standard complements: given sides determine third; given an acute angle gives complement; tables follow enumerating cases and proportional relations (sine/tangent relations) to resolve the five principal right-triangle cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Proposition (oblique triangle cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: In an oblique-angled triangle, of the three sides and three angles, any three being given, the other three may be found, except when the three angles are given (only ratios of sides then given).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presents methods/cases using the law relating sides to sines, tangents of sums/differences, and constructions with altitude AD; notes ambiguous case with two possible solutions when certain inequalities hold (two solutions when an angle may be greater or less than a quadrant). Tables and algebraic forms are given to compute unknowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spherical Definitions I–IV (pole, great circle, spherical triangle/angle)
rubrics_metrics.description: I: Pole of a circle on sphere — point from which all straight lines to circumference are equal. II: Great circle — plane passes through centre of sphere. III: Spherical triangle — figure on sphere bounded by three arcs of great circles each less than semicircle. IV: Spherical angle — angle contained by two arcs of great circles, equal to inclination of their planes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions set the foundational vocabulary for spherical trigonometry; used to define arcs as measures and to derive relations between spherical arcs, poles, and quadrants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spherical Proposition I (great circles bisect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Great circles bisect one another: their common section is a diameter of each which bisects them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate from common centre property; useful for constructing midpoints and bisected arcs on sphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spherical Proposition II (pole–circumference quadrant)
rubrics_metrics.description: The arch of a great circle between the pole and the circumference of another is a quadrant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ABC is great circle and D its pole, any great circle through D meeting ABC yields arcs DA and DC which are quadrants. Proof uses equalities of segments from pole and central symmetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spherical Proposition III (measure of spherical angle)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a great circle described meets two great circles AB, AC passing through its pole A in B,C, the angle at the centre of the sphere upon circumference BC is the same with the spherical angle BAC, and the arch BC is called the measure of the spherical angle BAC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relates spherical angle measure to central angle at sphere centre; corollary: through pole A, two quadrants AB, AC determine BC whose pole is A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spherical Proposition IV (isosceles spherical triangle base angles equal)
rubrics_metrics.description: In isosceles spherical triangles the angles at the base are equal (if two sides are equal, the base angles are equal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses centre of sphere and symmetry arguments, constructing perpendiculars and equalities in plane sections to deduce equality of base angles.
